items.q: The static equilibrium of a pile at failure gives
items.why: Downward: P<sub>u</sub> and the pile weight W. Upward: shaft resistance P<sub>s</sub> and base resistance P<sub>b</sub>. So P<sub>u</sub> = P<sub>s</sub> + P<sub>b</sub> − W.

items.q: If the pile weight is assumed equal to the overburden removed (W = p<sub>o</sub>A<sub>b</sub>), the capacity becomes
items.why: The p<sub>o</sub>A<sub>b</sub> in the base term cancels the −W term, leaving the shaft and the net base resistance.

items.q: A driven precast concrete pile is classified as a
items.why: Driving pushes soil aside (large displacement). Bored cast-in-place piles remove soil first (non-displacement); H-piles and screw piles are small-displacement.

items.q: A pile that carries its load mainly by friction along the shaft, with little at the base, is called
items.why: End-bearing piles transfer load to a hard stratum at the base; floating piles use shaft and base within a soft deposit.

items.q: Reasons to choose piles over shallow foundations include

options.A: low column loads on a thick gravel
options.C: a deep, dense, uniform sand at the surface
options.D: very large loads, weak or compressible soil near the surface, scour, or a high water table

items.why: Piles carry load to deeper stiff strata or by skin friction, bypassing weak near-surface soil.

items.q: In pile design the two calculations that must both be checked are
items.why: As for shallow foundations: ultimate and serviceability limit states.

items.q: For a pile in clay under undrained loading the unit shaft friction is

options.B: f<sub>s</sub> = αc<sub>u</sub>, with α ≤ 1 depending on c<sub>u</sub>, pile type and installation

items.why: Adhesion c<sub>a</sub> = αc<sub>u</sub> (α from the AS 2159 chart: 1.0 at low c<sub>u</sub>, falling at high c<sub>u</sub>). Kσ′tanδ is the sand expression, 2N̄ the Meyerhof sand relation.

items.q: The base resistance of a long pile (L/D ≥ 4) in clay is f<sub>b</sub> =

options.C: 9c<sub>u</sub>, with c<sub>u</sub> averaged over about 2D below the base
options.D: 9c<sub>u</sub> with c<sub>u</sub> at the ground surface

items.why: Skempton: N<sub>c</sub> = 9 for L/D ≥ 4 (chart below that). The base acts like a deep footing, so the strength 2D below the base counts.

items.q: A 0.6 m diameter pile, 10 m long, in uniform clay with c<sub>u</sub> = 50 kPa (α = 0.88 for this c<sub>u</sub>), N<sub>c</sub> = 9. Neglect the pile weight and overburden at the base. P<sub>u</sub> is about
items.why: P<sub>s</sub> = αc<sub>u</sub>πDL = 0.88·50·π·0.6·10 = 829 kN; P<sub>b</sub> = 9c<sub>u</sub>πD²/4 = 127 kN; P<sub>u</sub> = 957 kN.

items.q: A pile shaft (D = 0.5 m) crosses two clay layers: 4 m with c<sub>u</sub> = 30 kPa (α = 1) and 6 m with c<sub>u</sub> = 60 kPa (α = 0.8). The shaft resistance is
items.why: Layer by layer: P<sub>s</sub> = πD·Σα c<sub>u</sub>L = π·0.5·(30·4 + 0.8·60·6) = π·0.5·408 = 641 kN. The week 7 slides mark the layered method for the test and exam.

items.q: The week 7 slides give three ways to find P<sub>s</sub> when c<sub>u</sub> varies with depth. The one marked for the test and exam is

options.A: a full integral of αc<sub>u</sub>πD dz
options.B: dividing the shaft into layers, each with its average c<sub>u</sub> and α
options.C: one average c<sub>u</sub> and α for the whole shaft
options.D: using c<sub>u</sub> at the base only

items.why: "Method 2 for test/exam": layers with their own average c<sub>u</sub> and α.

items.q: Why is the strength 2D below the base, not at the base, used for N<sub>c</sub>c<sub>u</sub>?

options.C: The failure zone beneath the base extends about 2D, so the soil there supports the pile
options.D: It is a safety factor of 2

items.why: Base resistance is a bearing capacity, mobilised in the soil in the failure zone below the base.

items.q: For a pile in sand (drained analysis) the unit shaft friction is
items.why: Mohr–Coulomb at the interface: f<sub>s</sub> = c<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>n</sub>tanδ with c<sub>a</sub> = 0 and σ<sub>n</sub> = σ′<sub>h</sub> = Kσ′<sub>v</sub>.

items.q: The interface friction angle δ is

options.A: generally less than the soil friction angle φ, depending on the pile material

items.why: Rough concrete gives δ/φ ≈ 1; smooth steel only 0.5 to 0.7.

items.q: For a normally consolidated sand with φ<sub>cs</sub> = 30°, the at-rest coefficient K<sub>o</sub> = 1 − sinφ is
items.why: 1 − sin 30° = 0.5. The pile K is K<sub>o</sub> times a factor (e.g. 1 for a dense driven pile).

items.q: The pile coefficient K is, relative to K<sub>o</sub>, largest for

options.C: a driven pile in soft/loose soil (K/K<sub>o</sub> up to 2)

items.why: Driving displaces and densifies the soil, raising the horizontal stress; boring or jetting lowers it (K/K<sub>o</sub> ≈ 2/3 to 3/4).

items.q: Meyerhof (1959) for driven piles in granular soil: f<sub>s</sub> = 2N̄ (kPa). For N̄ = 17,
items.why: f<sub>s</sub> = 2·17 = 34 kPa.

items.q: Meyerhof: f<sub>b</sub> = 40N<sub>b</sub>L/D ≤ 400N<sub>b</sub> kPa. For N<sub>b</sub> = 20 and L/D = 10 the base resistance is
items.why: 40·20·10 = 8000 = 400·20, exactly at the cap.

items.q: In the Meyerhof base relation f<sub>b</sub> = 40N<sub>b</sub>L/D, the cap 400N<sub>b</sub> applies because

options.B: beyond L/D = 10 the base resistance stops increasing (critical depth)

items.why: Resistance does not increase indefinitely with depth; the limit is reached at L/D = 10.

items.q: The N used in the Meyerhof relations is

options.C: the SPT count of the 2nd + 3rd 150 mm of drive, averaged over the shaft for f<sub>s</sub> and near the base for f<sub>b</sub>

items.why: N̄ over the shaft for f<sub>s</sub>; N<sub>b</sub> around the base for f<sub>b</sub>.

items.q: Using the critical-state friction angle φ<sub>cs</sub> instead of the peak φ<sub>p</sub> in design is

options.D: more conservative, because φ<sub>cs</sub> < φ<sub>p</sub> for dense sand

items.why: At large strains dense sand softens to φ<sub>cs</sub>; peak values overestimate capacity if the soil strains a lot.

items.q: The recommended minimum spacing S (centre to centre) between piles in a group is
items.why: Closer spacing overlaps the stress bulbs and reduces group efficiency.

items.q: The capacity of a group of floating piles is taken as

options.B: the lesser of n·P<sub>u</sub> and the equivalent block capacity P<sub>u,b</sub>

items.why: Two failure modes: individual piles, or the block of piles and soil. The weaker governs.

items.q: A 3 × 3 group of piles with P<sub>u</sub> = 580 kN each, and an equivalent block capacity of 15 000 kN. The group capacity and the load for FS = 3 are
items.why: n·P<sub>u</sub> = 9·580 = 5220 kN < 15 000, so governs; P<sub>a</sub> = 5220/3 = 1740 kN.

items.q: The equivalent block of a clay group: B = W = 3 m, L = 10 m, c<sub>a</sub> = 40 kPa, c<sub>u,base</sub> = 60 kPa, N<sub>c</sub> = 9. P<sub>u,b</sub> = c<sub>a</sub>·2(B + W)L + N<sub>c</sub>c<sub>u</sub>BW is
items.why: Skin on the block perimeter: 40·2(3 + 3)·10 = 4800 kN; base: 9·60·3·3 = 4860 kN. Sum = 9660 kN.

items.q: In the equivalent block (clay) analysis the soil-to-soil side shear on the block is

options.A: not reduced: c<sub>a</sub> is the soil c<sub>u</sub> because the failure surface lies in soil
options.B: reduced by α like a pile

items.why: "No reduction on c<sub>u</sub> required" for the soil–soil interface.

items.q: For a group of end-bearing piles on rock, the group capacity is

options.B: n·P<sub>u,single</sub>, set by the base resistance

items.why: Each pile bears on the hard layer, so the piles act independently.

items.q: A hollow (open-ended) pile has the soil plug inside. Its base capacity, if the pile is not too thin,

options.C: is not reduced by the hollow core

items.why: The soil inside the pile supports load too, so the base is treated as a full section.

items.q: Group efficiency η = P<sub>u,g</sub>/(nP<sub>u</sub>). Four piles each with P<sub>u</sub> = 1000 kN and a block capacity of 3200 kN give η =
In Poulos' elastic solution the settlement of a single floating pile under load P is

options.A: S = P·I/(E<sub>s</sub>·D), I from the stiffness factor K and L/D

items.why: I is an influence factor read against K and L/D, with corrections R<sub>v</sub> and R<sub>h</sub> as needed.

items.q: A solid steel pile (E<sub>p</sub> = 200 GPa, R<sub>A</sub> = 1) in soil with E<sub>s</sub> = 200 MPa. The stiffness factor K = (E<sub>p</sub>/E<sub>s</sub>)R<sub>A</sub> is
items.why: 200 000 MPa/200 MPa = 1000, times R<sub>A</sub> = 1.

items.q: P = 2000 kN, D = 1.0 m, E<sub>s</sub> = 200 MPa, I = 1.4 (L/D = 10, K = 1000). S = PI/(E<sub>s</sub>D) is
P = 2500 kN, D = 1.2 m, E<sub>s</sub> = 200 MPa, I = 1.8, R<sub>v</sub> = 0.94, R<sub>h</sub> = 0.82. The settlement is
R<sub>h</sub> < 1 corrects the settlement for

options.A: a rigid layer at finite depth h below the pile, which reduces settlement

items.why: A stiff base within the influence zone stiffens the system; the pile settles less than in an infinite half-space.

items.q: R<sub>v</sub> (Poisson's ratio correction) is applied when

options.B: the soil is compressible, ν < 0.5 (the chart is for ν = 0.5)

items.why: The basic solution assumes an incompressible soil (ν = 0.5); R<sub>v</sub> adjusts for a real ν.

items.q: An end-bearing pile on rock: the settlement is mainly the elastic shortening, S = MR·PL/(A<sub>p</sub>E<sub>p</sub>). P = 1000 kN, L = 20 m, A<sub>p</sub> = 0.2 m², E<sub>p</sub> = 30 GPa, MR = 0.8 gives
items.why: 0.8·1000·20/(0.2·30 000 000) = 0.00267 m. MR (movement ratio) comes from K and L/D.

items.q: The settlement of a pile in a group is found by

options.C: multiplying the single pile settlement by n
options.D: superposition: its own settlement plus the effect of each neighbour (interaction factors)

items.why: S<sub>k</sub> = S<sub>o</sub>(P<sub>k</sub> + Σ α<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub>); it needs linear elastic behaviour and small deformation.

items.q: The interaction factor α between two piles is

options.A: the extra settlement caused by the neighbour under unit load, divided by the settlement of a single pile under unit load

items.why: It is dimensionless and falls with spacing s/D.

items.q: Two identical piles each carry 1000 kN. One pile alone under 1000 kN settles 10 mm; the interaction factor is 0.4. The settlement of each pile in the group is
items.why: S = 10 + 0.4·10 = 14 mm (S<sub>o</sub>P + αS<sub>o</sub>P).

items.q: Four identical piles at the corners of a square each carry the same load; a single pile alone settles 8 mm. Interaction factors: 0.5 to each adjacent pile (two) and 0.35 to the diagonal. Each pile in the group settles
As the pile spacing s/D increases, the interaction factor

options.D: decreases, so group settlement approaches that of a single pile

items.why: Neighbours influence each other less when farther apart.

items.q: The superposition principle used for pile groups is exact only if

options.A: the soil is linear elastic and the deformations are small

items.why: Linear elasticity is needed for the effects to add; otherwise it is an approximation, "better than nothing".

items.q: A group of piles under the same load per pile settles

options.A: the same as a single pile
options.B: more than a single pile, because of interaction

items.why: Each pile feels its neighbours: Σα > 0 adds settlement.

items.q: In a piled raft foundation

options.A: the piles carry all the load and the raft none
options.B: the piles act only as tension anchors
options.C: the raft and the piles share the load, piles mainly reducing settlement and differential settlement
options.D: the raft carries all the load

items.why: Piled raft: load carried partly by the raft contact and partly by the piles.

items.q: A piled raft is not suitable when

options.D: the surface soil is very soft clay or very loose sand (the raft can lose contact)

items.why: Contact support from very soft or loose soil is small or lost, so the piles would carry everything.

items.q: Increasing the number of piles in a piled raft

options.A: lowers settlement, but the benefit per pile decreases once the number passes a critical value

items.why: Diminishing returns: efficiency of the piles falls after a point.

items.q: Poulos suggested a three-stage design: preliminary design, assessment of piling requirement, and
items.why: The lecture stresses that simple spreadsheet methods are only for a rough estimate; advanced numerical analysis is needed in the final stage.

items.q: In AS 2159 the strength reduction factor φ<sub>g</sub> for the ultimate pile capacity is highest (0.70 to 0.90) when the capacity is assessed by

options.A: static analysis using laboratory data (cohesive soil)
options.D: static analysis using SPT data (cohesionless soil)

items.why: The better the direct measurement, the higher φ<sub>g</sub>: static test to failure 0.70–0.90, CPT 0.45–0.65, lab data 0.45–0.55, SPT 0.40–0.55.

items.q: In limit-state (LRFD) design with AS 1170 load factors, the design action for dead load G and live load Q is
items.why: S* = 1.25G + 1.5Q is the dead + live combination quoted in the lecture; R* = φ<sub>g</sub>R<sub>u</sub> must be at least S*.

items.q: A pile has R<sub>u</sub> = 2000 kN from static analysis with SPT data, φ<sub>g</sub> = 0.5. The design capacity R* is
items.why: R* = φ<sub>g</sub>R<sub>u</sub> = 0.5·2000 = 1000 kN. With G = 300 kN, Q = 400 kN, S* = 1.25·300 + 1.5·400 = 975 kN, so it just passes.

items.q: In working-stress design, the overall factor of safety on pile capacity is typically in the range
items.why: The lecture quotes 2 to 5; 2.5 to 3 is used in the examples.

items.q: Which method for the pile ultimate capacity is called the most important in the course?
items.why: The lecture: static methods are "the" foundation for all calculations on pile foundations.

items.q: The lecture example: D = 1.3 m, L = 12 m, c<sub>u</sub> by layers with α = 1, 1 and 0.88 over 2, 5 and 5 m (average c<sub>u</sub> 30, 30 and 50 kPa). Method 2 gives P<sub>s</sub> =
items.why: P<sub>s</sub> = πD·Σαc<sub>u</sub>L = π·1.3·(30·2 + 30·5 + 0.88·50·5) = π·1.3·430. The slide takes π ≈ 3 (3·1.3·430 = 1677 ≈ 1700 kN; exact π gives 1756). With P<sub>b</sub> = 700 kN, P<sub>u</sub> = 2400 kN (method 1, one average layer, gave 2600).
